title: Ezekiel 40:38–49
context: Near the inner gates are a room for washing the burnt offering and eight tables for slaughtering offerings, including four tables of cut stone, a cubit and a half long and wide and one cubit high. Rooms in the inner court belong to the singers and to two groups of priests: those who keep charge of the house and those who keep charge of the altar, the sons of Zadok. The inner court is a square of one hundred cubits with the altar before the house. Finally, the guide measures the porch of the house, with pillars beside its posts. The mention of sacrifices raises a question readers handle differently. Some who expect a literal future temple see memorial or purifying offerings, while others read the sacrifices as Ezekiel's picture of restored worship in the terms of his day, fulfilled in Christ's “one sacrifice for sins forever” (Hebrews 10:12). Both views are held among Arminian and Reformed readers.

verses.text: A room with its door was by the posts at the gates. They washed the burnt offering there.
verses.arminianNotes: “A room with its door was by the posts at the gates.” Arminian readers see a room set apart for washing, since “They washed the burnt offering there.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the vision includes the practical means of worship as well as its structure. Readers differ on whether the sacrifices are literal or symbolic.

verses.text: In the porch of the gate were two tables on this side and two tables on that side, on which to kill the burnt offering, the sin offering, and the trespass offering.
verses.arminianNotes: “In the porch of the gate were two tables on this side and two tables on that side.” Arminian readers see tables for slaughtering “the burnt offering, the sin offering, and the trespass offering.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that these offerings are familiar from the law of Moses. Many read them in light of Hebrews 10:12, while others expect them in a literal future temple. Both readings appear in each tradition.

verses.text: On the one side outside, as one goes up to the entry of the gate toward the north, were two tables; and on the other side, which belonged to the porch of the gate, were two tables.
verses.arminianNotes: “On the one side outside, as one goes up to the entry of the gate toward the north, were two tables.” Arminian readers see more tables beside the north gate, placed both outside and in the porch.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the exact placement of these tables is not fully clear. The general picture is of a gate equipped for sacrificial worship.

verses.text: Four tables were on this side, and four tables on that side, by the side of the gate: eight tables, on which they killed the sacrifices.
verses.arminianNotes: “Four tables were on this side, and four tables on that side.” Arminian readers see a total of “eight tables, on which they killed the sacrifices,” showing an orderly provision for worship.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the count and arrangement show care for worship done properly. The orderliness fits the vision's concern for holiness throughout.

verses.text: There were four cut stone tables for the burnt offering, a cubit and a half long, a cubit and a half wide, and one cubit high. They laid the instruments with which they killed the burnt offering and the sacrifice on them.
verses.arminianNotes: “There were four cut stone tables for the burnt offering.” Arminian readers see small stone tables, a cubit and a half square and a cubit high, where the instruments for sacrifice were laid.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the precise measures given in cubits. These smaller tables complete the furnishings near the gate, prepared for the work of the priests.

verses.text: The hooks, a hand width long, were fastened within all around. The meat of the offering was on the tables.
verses.arminianNotes: “The hooks, a hand width long, were fastened within all around.” Arminian readers see hooks fixed in the room and the meat of the offering laid on the tables.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that even small details are recorded. The vision treats every part of worship as belonging to the LORD's ordered house.

verses.text: Outside of the inner gate were rooms for the singers in the inner court, which was at the side of the north gate. They faced toward the south. One at the side of the east gate faced toward the north.
verses.arminianNotes: “Outside of the inner gate were rooms for the singers in the inner court.” Arminian readers see rooms provided for those who led worship in song, beside the north and east gates.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that singing had a set place in Israel's worship, as the historical books describe. The mention here shows praise as part of restored worship.

verses.text: He said to me, “This room, which faces toward the south, is for the priests who perform the duty of the house.
verses.arminianNotes: He said to me, “This room, which faces toward the south, is for the priests who perform the duty of the house.” Arminian readers see the guide explaining the rooms' purpose.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the guide speaks to interpret the vision for the prophet. The priests who keep charge of the house have their own place in the court.

verses.text: The room which faces toward the north is for the priests who perform the duty of the altar. These are the sons of Zadok, who from among the sons of Levi come near to the LORD to minister to him.”
verses.arminianNotes: “The room which faces toward the north is for the priests who perform the duty of the altar.” Arminian readers see a second group of priests named as “the sons of Zadok,” who come near to minister.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Ezekiel 44:15 explains that the sons of Zadok were faithful “when the children of Israel went astray from me.” Faithfulness is honored with nearness to God.

verses.text: He measured the court, one hundred cubits long and one hundred cubits wide, square. The altar was before the house.
verses.arminianNotes: “He measured the court, one hundred cubits long and one hundred cubits wide, square.” Arminian readers see the inner court as a perfect square with “The altar was before the house.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the square shape and the central altar give the inner court a sense of completeness. Revelation 21:16 also describes a city that is square, though it is a different vision.

verses.text: Then he brought me to the porch of the house, and measured each post of the porch, five cubits on this side, and five cubits on that side. The width of the gate was three cubits on this side and three cubits on that side.
verses.arminianNotes: “Then he brought me to the porch of the house.” Arminian readers see the prophet brought to the threshold of the temple building itself, with its posts measured at five cubits on each side.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the tour has moved from the outer wall to the house itself. The approach is gradual, marked by rising steps and narrowing spaces.

verses.text: The length of the porch was twenty cubits and the width eleven cubits, even by the steps by which they went up to it. There were pillars by the posts, one on this side, and another on that side.
verses.arminianNotes: “The length of the porch was twenty cubits and the width eleven cubits.” Arminian readers see the porch reached by steps, with “pillars by the posts, one on this side, and another on that side.”
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Solomon's temple also had two pillars at its porch (1 Kings 7:21). The vision recalls the earlier temple while describing a new one.
